title: Meta delays terms that let it crawl business sites; robots.txt status unclear
why: Expected: robots.txt settles crawler permission. Found: Meta's business terms grant crawling by contract, and they do not say whether robots.txt limits that grant.
source_check: Checked 27 Oct 2026. The article confirms Oct 30 moved to Nov 20 (U.S. English previews list Nov 20), WAN-IFRA asked Meta to temporarily stop the crawling provision for news publishers and to make robots.txt binding, and that the new terms do not say whether robots.txt limits the grant. The article shows no publication date of its own (only '14 hours ago' and 'Copyright 2026'); our feed records it on 26 Oct 2026. The Oct 19 SEJ article in the earlier note was not opened and is not cited.
status: do not publish until the owner approves

drafts.text: Meta moved its updated business terms from Oct 30 to Nov 20. The permission to crawl sites tied to business users stays. The terms do not say whether robots.txt limits that grant. A robots.txt line is a preference. A contract can say something else.
thread: Mechanism: robots.txt is a convention crawlers choose to follow. Terms you accept in an ad account are an agreement. The two can point in different directions, and the published terms do not settle which one wins.
WAN-IFRA has asked Meta to temporarily stop the crawling provision for news publishers, and to make robots.txt binding inside the terms. As of Oct 25, some regional previews still showed Oct 30.

Monday morning: read the crawling paragraph in the new terms, then check what your robots.txt says for each Meta crawler. Source: https://www.searchenginejournal.com/meta-delays-business-terms-crawling/594388/ (Search Engine Journal, feed date 26 Oct 2026).

drafts.text:
Meta has delayed its updated business terms from Oct 30 to Nov 20, according to Search Engine Journal. The clause that lets Meta crawl sites tied to business users is still in both agreements.

Meta says site owners can state crawling preferences in robots.txt. The terms I could read do not say whether a robots.txt rule limits what a business has agreed to grant. WAN-IFRA has asked for that to be written in.

The gap is worth knowing about. A robots.txt rule is a preference a crawler chooses to honor. Terms you accept are a contract. If you run ads, those are two separate places where crawling is decided.

What I would do this week: read the crawling paragraph, and check how your robots.txt treats each Meta crawler. I am not a lawyer, and this is a reading of press coverage, not of the final terms.

Method note: based on one trade report (Search Engine Journal, feed date 26 Oct 2026). Confidence: medium on the dates, low on how the clause will work.
